article_title: Using Data to Ensure That Teachers Are Learner Ready on Day One
citation: Data Quality Campaign. (2017). Using Data to Ensure That Teachers Are Learner Ready on Day One. https://www.dataqualitycampaign.org
title: AACTE and Westat pilot survey of beginning teachers and their supervisors
description: In spring 2017 the American Association of Colleges for Teacher Education and Westat piloted a new state survey instrument for beginning teachers and their supervisors. Developed with input from state partners, it "aims to provide more detailed information about graduates' experiences in the classroom and help states make more meaningful comparisons across programs." The instrument is intended to give EPPs and states better information about graduates' performance and needs than existing collections provide.
requirements: Developed with input from state partners so the questions meet state stakeholder needs
target_learners: beginning teachers (teachers of record in their first years)
target_learning_goals: informing EPP program improvement and state comparisons of preparation program quality
examples: Piloted in spring 2017 for beginning teachers and their supervisors
key_sources: Data Quality Campaign. (2017). Using Data to Ensure That Teachers Are Learner Ready on Day One. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED586474

article_title: Judgment-Centred Software Engineering Education: A Post-Hype Review and Framework for AI-Augmented Learning
citation: Qusay H. Mahmoud. (2026). Judgment-Centred Software Engineering Education: A Post-Hype Review and Framework for AI-Augmented Learning. Preprint, September 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.29473
title: AASEE framework: five non-linear AI integration levels crossed by four evidence-of-learning obligations (explain, verify, modify, account)
description: The AI-Augmented Software Engineering Education (AASEE) framework connects the scope of delegated engineering work and its lifecycle consequence to observable evidence of retained human competence. "Table 2 summarizes the five AASEE integration levels, their educational focus, typical forms of delegation, and the evidence or safeguards associated with each": tool awareness, guardrailed AI-assisted development, AI-collaborative engineering, AI governance, and agentic and AI systems engineering. Across all levels, four obligations—explain, verify, modify, and account—make retained competence visible; "Together, these obligations shift assessment from visible authorship to visible judgment". Levels are selected from the learning objective, not pursued as a maturity ladder.
requirements: Learning objectives are stated without reference to a tool before choosing an integration level
Evidence obligations (explanation, independent verification, modification under changed conditions, provenance and accountability) must accompany any delegation
constraints: Higher levels are not inherently better; a first-year tracing exercise may remain AI-restricted even where agent orchestration is taught elsewhere
Agentic curriculum proposals are not yet validated learning models
examples: A testing course at Level 3 has students obtain an initial test suite from an LLM, then classify the input space, justify oracles, add cases, and respond to a seeded defect or change request
A capstone combining Levels 4 and 5 defines task boundaries, permissions, sandboxes, acceptance tests, review ownership, and a recovery plan before an agent touches a repository
key_sources: Qusay H. Mahmoud. (2026). Judgment-Centred Software Engineering Education: A Post-Hype Review and Framework for AI-Augmented Learning. Preprint, September 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.29473

article_title: Effect of Computer-Based Multimedia Presentation on Senior Secondary Students' Achievement in Agricultural Science
citation: Abiola Lateef Olori and Adekunle Olusegun Igbosanu. (2016). Effect of Computer- Based Multimedia Presentation on Senior Secondary Students’ Achievement in Agricultural Science. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.31. https://www.iiste.org
title: Agriculture Achievement Test (AAT), a 20-item multiple-choice instrument
description: The AAT is a measurement instrument self-developed by the researchers, consisting of "20 multiple choice test items based on the topics in this study (maize husbandry)". It was validated by experts in Educational Evaluation and Agricultural Science for face and content validity, and subjected to test-retest, yielding a reliability coefficient of 0.85 using the Kuder Richardson (KR 20) method. It was administered for one hour as both pre-test and post-test to both groups.
requirements: Face and content validity established by experts in Educational Evaluation and Agricultural Science
Reliability of 0.85 established via test-retest using the KR 20 method
target_learners: Senior Secondary School Two (SS II) agriculture students
target_learning_goals: Achievement in agricultural science (maize husbandry topics)
examples: Administered as a one-hour pre-test in week two and a one-hour post-test in week four of the four-week study
key_sources: Abiola Lateef Olori and Adekunle Olusegun Igbosanu. (2016). Effect of Computer- Based Multimedia Presentation on Senior Secondary Students’ Achievement in Agricultural Science. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.31. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1122547

article_title: Effects of Reflective Thinking in the Process of Designing Software on Students' Learning Performances
citation: Hsieh, P.-H., & Chen, N.-S. (2012). Effects of reflective thinking in the process of designing software on students' learning performances. Computers & Education, 58(1), 419-431. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2011.12.021
title: AACSB's five multi-dimensional assessment criteria for a software design course: Information Technology, Oral Communication, Problem Solving, Value and Professionalism, and Creativity and Innovation.
description: This study evaluates students' learning performances according to AACSB's five criteria developed for a software design course: Information Technology (IT), Oral Communication (OC), Problem Solving (PS), Value and Professionalism (VP), and Creativity and Innovation (CI), with different percentage weights. Each criterion has specified sub-criteria, such as debugging software from error codes (the most important PS one).
requirements: Based on the goals established according to the course syllabus, each criterion score had a specific weight
constraints: design principle may have application in some, but not a ll, design projects
examples: Evaluations included scores for three kinds of design scores from quizzes, homework, one midterm exam, one final exam, a design work, and oral and written presentations for the design work
key_sources: Hsieh, P.-H., & Chen, N.-S. (2012). Effects of reflective thinking in the process of designing software on students' learning performances. Computers & Education, 58(1), 419-431. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2011.12.021

article_title: What Is Needed for Correct Pronunciation: A Model or a Concern?
citation: Kayaoglu, M. N. & Caylak, N. (2013). What is needed for correct pronunciation: a model or a concern? Eurasian Journal of Educational Research, 53, 269-290. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1075217
title: A single-session pronunciation method should be treated as a complementary tool, not a complete pronunciation curriculum
description: The Audio Articulation Method targets segmental-level pronunciation errors within one or two class hours, but the article concludes it "addresses a very limited part of the pronunciation issues and does not include stress, rhythm, intonation, connected speech, or prominence." Because it also lacks built-in feedback and automatization mechanisms, the authors recommend it be used alongside a broader pronunciation lesson rather than as a standalone method.
requirements: Requires follow-up with controlled practice, guided practice, and communicative practice with accompanying feedback to sustain lasting change
constraints: Addresses only segmental-level errors; does not cover suprasegmental features such as stress, rhythm, intonation, connected speech, or prominence
target_learners: Adult EFL learners at elementary level
target_learning_goals: Correct pronunciation of problematic segmental sounds
Phonological awareness of target language sounds
examples: The experimental group received three 45-minute AAM lessons with videos, songs, games, PowerPoint presentations, discrimination activities, dialogue performances, and mirrors for visual feedback
key_sources: Kayaoglu, M. N. & Caylak, N. (2013). What is needed for correct pronunciation: a model or a concern? Eurasian Journal of Educational Research, 53, 269-290. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1060386

article_title: Beyond AI Detection: A Decision-Making Guide for Strategic Assessment Design in Nursing Education.
citation: McCusker KA, Kennedy BB, Parish A. (2026). Beyond AI Detection: A Decision-Making Guide for Strategic Assessment Design in Nursing Education. Nurse Educator. https://doi.org/10.1097/NNE.0000000000002281
title: AAAE framework: Against, Avoid, Adapt, Explore — instructors' philosophical responses to AI in assessment
description: The article cites Khlaif et al's AAAE framework, which captures "the spectrum of instructors' philosophical responses to AI in assessment design" across four positions: Against, Avoid, Adapt, and Explore. The article values its conceptual categories but notes it "does not provide actionable guidance for evaluating specific assessments," a gap the decision-making guide addresses.
requirements: Provides conceptual categories for understanding faculty positions
constraints: Does not provide actionable guidance for evaluating specific assessments or determining appropriate assessment strategies based on context and/or stakes
target_learning_goals: understanding faculty positions on AI in assessment design
key_sources: McCusker KA, Kennedy BB, Parish A. (2026). Beyond AI Detection: A Decision-Making Guide for Strategic Assessment Design in Nursing Education. Nurse Educator. https://doi.org/10.1097/NNE.0000000000002281

article_title: Comparing diagnostic skills in endodontic cases: dental students versus ChatGPT-4o.
citation: Durmazpinar Parla Meva, Ekmekci Ece. (2025). Comparing diagnostic skills in endodontic cases: dental students versus ChatGPT-4o. BMC Oral Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12903-025-05857-y
title: AAE-guideline-based 15-question endodontic diagnostic assessment with radiographs, clinical photographs and patient histories
description: An instrument of 15 multiple-choice questions built from real patient cases at the Marmara University Endodontics Clinic, using "patient histories, panoramic and periapical radiographs, and clinical photographs". Questions were structured on the American Association of Endodontists' Clinical Endodontics Guidelines, reviewed by two experienced endodontists who reached consensus, and pilot-tested by students for clarity before distribution via Google Forms. Responses were scored as correct, incorrect, or unanswered against the AAE Guide to Clinical Endodontics.
requirements: Questions calibrated by two experienced endodontists through expert consensus
Pilot testing with students for clarity and comprehensibility
Real patient cases with informed consent for image use
constraints: Based on a narrow range of clinical cases from a single endodontics clinic
Multiple-choice format only, limiting insight into open-ended performance
target_learning_goals: endodontic diagnosis of pulp and peri-radicular tissue diseases
examples: A researcher presented the same 15 questions to ChatGPT-4o 75 times while students answered once via Google Forms
key_sources: Durmazpinar Parla Meva, Ekmekci Ece. (2025). Comparing diagnostic skills in endodontic cases: dental students versus ChatGPT-4o. BMC Oral Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12903-025-05857-y

article_title: Virtual patients versus standardized patients for improving clinical reasoning skills in ophthalmology residents. A randomized controlled trial.
citation: Malik Tayyaba Gul, Mahboob Usman, Khan Rehan Ahmed, Alam Rabia. (2024). Virtual patients versus standardized patients for improving clinical reasoning skills in ophthalmology residents. A randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05241-4
title: American Academy of Ophthalmology virtual patient scenarios as a clinical reasoning exercise for ophthalmology residents
description: This element is the set of virtual patients selected from the American Academy of Ophthalmology website and used as the intervention in the trial. A VP is described as "a computer program in which real-life scenarios are presented as digital patients", in which the trainee acts as the doctor, takes history, chooses investigations and reaches a diagnosis and management plan in a safe environment. Each exercise lasted 30 to 45 minutes, with a second chance allowed after an incorrect final diagnosis.
requirements: Cases must be matched to residency year, as "depending on the case difficulty, residents were provided with different cases in different years"; permission from the content provider is needed, obtained by formal email to the Academy.
constraints: The article notes VPs are specialty specific and that "Bed side manners, patient welfare, communication skills cannot be taught by VP."
target_learners: Postgraduate ophthalmology residents (all four training years, mean age 28.5 ± 3)
target_learning_goals: Clinical reasoning skills: history taking, differential diagnosis, investigation selection, and diagnosis and management decisions
examples: Residents worked through clinical scenarios on the computer screen, chose relevant investigations, and gave a final diagnosis; the case ended if the answer was correct and allowed another chance if incorrect.
key_sources: Malik Tayyaba Gul, Mahboob Usman, Khan Rehan Ahmed, Alam Rabia. (2024). Virtual patients versus standardized patients for improving clinical reasoning skills in ophthalmology residents. A randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05241-4

article_title: The AaLplus near-peer teaching program in Family Medicine strengthens basic medical skills-A five-year retrospective study.
citation: Schwill Simon, Hundertmark Jan, Fahrbach-Veeser Johanna, Eicher Christiane, Tonchev Pencho, Kurczyk Sonia, Szecsenyi Joachim, Loukanova Svetla. (2020). The AaLplus near-peer teaching program in Family Medicine strengthens basic medical skills—A five-year retrospective study. PLoS ONE 15(5): e0233748. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0233748
title: AaLplus near-peer teaching program for preclinical basic medical skills
description: AaLplus (living anatomy plus) is a compulsory near-peer teaching program at Heidelberg University that "teaches basic medical skills, especially history taking, physical examination, and venepuncture, to preclinical students" across four semesters (320 students/year, 9h/semester, 30 hours total). Sessions occur in small groups of 10 to 12 participants led by teams of two tutors, using standardized patients, checklists, dummies, and case vignettes, and end with a formative OSCE with structured in-depth feedback.
requirements: Trained peer tutors who complete 40 to 50 hours of preparatory teaching training before teaching
Small groups of 10 to 12 participants to allow active participation and hands-on practical learning
Standardized patients selected, trained and supervised within the MediKIT program
constraints: The program is embedded in Heidelberg's longitudinal Family Medicine curriculum and aligned with other curricular blocks, so its structure is tied to that curriculum
Because the course is compulsory, no control group could be formed to compare the program's effect between participants
target_learners: Preclinical medical students in their first four semesters
target_learning_goals: Practical skills such as venepuncture, hand disinfection and blood pressure measurement
examples: In 2018, there were 101 applicants for 21 tutor positions; tutors teach in teams of two so novice tutors are supported by a senior tutor
key_sources: Schwill Simon, Hundertmark Jan, Fahrbach-Veeser Johanna, Eicher Christiane, Tonchev Pencho, Kurczyk Sonia, Szecsenyi Joachim, Loukanova Svetla. (2020). The AaLplus near-peer teaching program in Family Medicine strengthens basic medical skills—A five-year retrospective study. PLoS ONE 15(5): e0233748. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0233748

article_title: Promoting medical competencies through a didactic tutor qualification programme - a qualitative study based on the CanMEDS Physician Competency Framework.
citation: Homberg Angelika, Hundertmark Jan, Krause Jürgen, Brunnée Merle, Neumann Boris, Loukanova Svetla. (2019). Promoting medical competencies through a didactic tutor qualification programme – a qualitative study based on the CanMEDS Physician Competency Framework. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1636-5
title: Heidelberg AalPlus tutor qualification programme (four modules, about 40 teaching hours)
description: A structured didactic qualification programme preparing medical student tutors at Heidelberg Medical Faculty since 2010. "This programme consists of four modules: 1. medical didactics and group leadership, 2. subject-specific training, 3. performance of tutorial courses as well as 4. collegial advice and reflection on the tutors' activities." It comprises about 40 teaching hours on seven training days, and completers receive a Heidelberg Didactic Certificate for Tutors. Tutors then guide small groups of 10 to 12 preclinical students and serve as OSCE examiners.
requirements: Students' participation in the basic didactic and subject-specific training is a requirement in order to be able to start working as tutor
Candidates have to be at least in the third study year and pass a multi-step recruitment process
target_learners: Medical student tutors from higher semesters at Heidelberg Medical Faculty
target_learning_goals: Subject-specific teaching of clinical and practical skills
examples: Tutors are trained to teach anatomy, sonography, practical skills, anamnesis and physical examination within the longitudinal, compulsory AalPlus courses
key_sources: Homberg Angelika, Hundertmark Jan, Krause Jürgen, Brunnée Merle, Neumann Boris, Loukanova Svetla. (2019). Promoting medical competencies through a didactic tutor qualification programme – a qualitative study based on the CanMEDS Physician Competency Framework. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1636-5

article_title: Physicians' lack of knowledge - a possible reason for red blood cell transfusion overuse?
citation: Rahav Koren Roni, Suriu Celia, Yakir Orly, Akria Luiza, Barhoum Masad, Braester Andrei. (2017). Physicians' lack of knowledge - a possible reason for red blood cell transfusion overuse? Israel Journal of Health Policy Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13584-017-0173-0
title: AABB-guideline-based transfusion medicine knowledge questionnaire
description: A validated questionnaire used to assess physicians' knowledge of transfusion medicine, based on the AABB guideline. It contains a personal background section (8 questions) and a professional section (20 questions) examining general knowledge, familiarity with restrictive blood management (eight questions), and indications for transfusion (six questions). Scores are the proportion of correct answers multiplied by 100, ranging 0-100. The questionnaire "was validated by peer review of the three hematologists at our institute with the greatest interest in transfusion medicine", and a 9-questionnaire pilot study yielded a Cronbach alpha of 0.7.
requirements: Peer review validation by transfusion-medicine hematologists
Pilot testing to demonstrate validity and reliability
constraints: The authors note open-ended instead of multiple choice questions could overcome randomly correct answers and possibly be more informative
target_learners: physicians in internal medicine and surgical departments
target_learning_goals: assessment of transfusion medicine knowledge, restrictive blood management familiarity, and indications for transfusion
examples: Administered anonymously to 79 physicians at Galilee Medical Center during morning meetings from February 2014 through March 2014
key_sources: Rahav Koren Roni, Suriu Celia, Yakir Orly, Akria Luiza, Barhoum Masad, Braester Andrei. (2017). Physicians' lack of knowledge - a possible reason for red blood cell transfusion overuse? Israel Journal of Health Policy Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13584-017-0173-0
